claims: A solemn assembly in The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is used for sustaining a new Church President.
A solemn assembly in The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is used for dedicating temples.
A solemn assembly in The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints is used for special instruction.
Solemn assemblies are primarily used to sustain a newly called President of the Church.
In solemn assemblies, members are asked to stand and sustain the First Presidency.
In solemn assemblies, members are asked to stand and sustain the Quorum of the Twelve Apostles.
In solemn assemblies, members are asked to stand and sustain other senior leaders.
Sustaining in solemn assemblies is typically organized by quorums.
A solemn assembly was held during the Saturday morning session of the April 2026 general conference to sustain the new First Presidency.
A solemn assembly was held in April 2020 for the 200th anniversary of the First Vision.
The April 2020 solemn assembly included the Hosanna Shout.
The phrase of the Hosanna Shout comes from the Hebrew Bible.
The phrase represents special gatherings during the Passover and the Feast of Tabernacles.
The first modern solemn assembly was held at the Kirtland Temple dedication in 1836.
The practice of raising hands and standing to sustain the prophet began with President John Taylor.
President John Taylor followed a pattern set at the Kirtland Temple dedication.
In recent assemblies like April 2018, the Melchizedek Priesthood, Relief Society, Aaronic Priesthood, Young Women, and the entire congregation stand in sequence to provide their sustaining vote.
Some solemn assemblies include the Hosanna Shout.
The Hosanna Shout is not always part of the procedure.
